children.text: A mountain village in Ifugao where rice terraces unfold around the settlement like an amphitheater, one of the core areas of the UNESCO World Heritage "Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras." The experience of staying in a village unreachable by car, walking the paddy walls, and trekking out to Tappiya Falls is truly special.
Batad is a mountain village about
16km

east of Banaue's town center. The entire valley where the village sits forms a round amphitheater shape, and hundreds of tiers of rice terraces wrap around its slopes like rows of seats. It's one of the five areas inscribed as the UNESCO World Heritage "Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras" in
, and many travelers rate Batad's scenery even more highly than Banaue's.

What sets Batad's paddies apart is that the walls are built of stone. Unlike some parts of Banaue, where the walls are packed earth, Batad's slopes are so steep that stone walls support the terraces, giving each tier a clearly defined curve. The traditional Ifugao irrigation system — mountain forests soaking up water and releasing it through bamboo channels, tier by tier from the top of the terraces down — still functions exactly as it always has.

The road has recently been extended closer to the village, but the final stretch still has to be walked. So instead of car noise, all you hear in Batad is the sound of water in the irrigation channels, roosters crowing, and the voices of residents working the paddies. Simple guesthouses and restaurants are scattered around the village overlooking the terraces, and spending a night to watch the paddies change color from sunrise to sunset is the heart of a Batad trip.

You need a reasonable level of fitness to climb up and down hundreds of stone steps and narrow paddy walls, but no special climbing skill is required. Highly recommended for photography enthusiasts, people who enjoy slow travel, and travelers interested in indigenous community life.
Batad is a barangay in the municipality of Banaue, with 825 residents as of the
census. The village center sits at about
above sea level, and the terraces climb the slopes of the amphitheater to around

. Of the five World Heritage areas, only two are in the municipality of Banaue, Batad and Bangaan, while the terraces seen from the viewpoint in Banaue town were left off the listing because of the many modern buildings. After young people left for the cities and the paddies were neglected, the site was on the List of World Heritage in Danger from
to
. In
November 2025

, when Super Typhoon Uwan (international name Fung-wong) struck, landslides killed two residents and destroyed a little over 2 ha of paddies and one old irrigation channel, and residents are continuing the restoration through communal labor.

From the viewpoint above the village, you can take in the whole rice terrace curving around the valley at a glance. It looks most three-dimensional when morning sunlight falls across the paddies and when the shadows lengthen in the late afternoon.

blocks.title: Crossing the village along the paddy walls

children.text: Walking along the narrow stone paddy walls straight through the middle of the amphitheater is an experience only Batad offers. The footing is narrow and high, so go slowly and follow behind your guide.
About
1 hour
down steep stone steps and a mountain trail from the village, a waterfall about
high and a wide pool appear. The water is very cold but swimmable, and the climb back up is the real challenge of this route.
Thatched-roof raised houses still stand throughout the village. Some guesthouses offer the experience of spending a night in a traditional house.

blocks.title: An overnight stay at a Batad village guesthouse

children.text: Once day-trip visitors leave in the afternoon, the village grows quiet. The sunset spreading over the paddies at dusk, the stars at night, and the fog clearing at dawn are sights you can only see by staying overnight.

blocks.title: Stopping by the Bangaan Village viewpoint

children.text: Bangaan, a World Heritage village along the way to Batad, is a good short stop, letting you look down from a roadside viewpoint at a traditional house village clustered in the middle of the terraces.
Visiting during planting or harvest season lets you see residents working the terraces in the traditional way. Asking politely through your guide, you may also get to hear their stories.

blocks.title: Awa viewpoint and Patpat village trek

children.text: Climbing to Awa Viewpoint on the ridge opposite the amphitheater lays all of Batad's terraces out beneath your feet. The trail drops to the riverbed and then climbs steeply back up, so it takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours 30 minutes

one way, and since some stretches pass right beside cliff edges, going with a guide is recommended. On the way back you can come down through Patpat, a small village with a suspension bridge and sweet potato fields.

A day trip is possible, but you have to manage both the uphill return from the falls and the climb to Saddle Point in a single day, which is very tiring and means missing Batad's sunset and dawn views. If your schedule allows, one night's stay is recommended.

Shared jeepneys go into Batad from Banaue in the afternoon and come out of Batad in the morning, so if you rely on jeepneys alone, two nights is the most natural fit. If you have energy left, you can visit Awa Viewpoint and Patpat village with a guide instead of the Day 2 afternoon plan, but doing both that and Tappiya Falls on the same day is too much.
The overnight direct bus from Manila to Banaue (Ohayami Trans, Coda Lines, and others) takes about
8–10 hours
and costs about
. Buses usually leave at night and arrive in the early morning.
Ohayami Trans departs at
10 PM
from its office in Sampaloc, Manila (corner of Fajardo Street and Lacson Avenue), and the Manila-bound bus leaves Banaue at
. Online booking is available (

Coda Lines runs several departures from its Cubao terminal (corner of Monte de Piedad Street and Maryland Street) between
, and Manila-bound buses leave Banaue in the afternoon. Fares vary with bus class and fuel surcharge, so check the latest fare when you book.
By private car, take the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) and continue through Nueva Ecija, Dalton Pass (Nueva Vizcaya), and Lagawe to Banaue, about
350km
and
8–9 hours
. You can drive from Banaue to the end of the Batad road, but it is a narrow mountain road, so drive in daylight.
From Banaue's town center to Batad Saddle Point takes about
40–50 minutes
by car. A chartered tricycle costs about
, and a chartered jeepney or van costs
or more; splitting it among several people lowers the cost per person.

Shared jeepneys toward Batad tend to depart mostly in the afternoon and come back out in the morning, so the schedule is irregular. If you're staying overnight, a shared jeepney can work, but check the departure time at the tourist information center the day before.
A shared jeepney costs tourists about
per person. Shared vehicles leaving Batad for Banaue usually go by around
9 AM
, so on the day you head back, you need to be up at the end of the road early in the morning.
Shared jeepneys depart from near the Banaue public market, usually with one or two trips in the morning and one around
3 PM
. When you register at the Banaue tourist information center, ask about that day's departure time.
These days vehicles go past the Saddle Point to the end of the concrete road farther down toward the village. If you are instead dropped at the Batad Junction on the main road, you have to walk about
3km
uphill to the Saddle Point, so whether you charter or share, settle clearly in advance where you will be let off.

items.title: From the Saddle Point to the village

children.text: From the end of the road to the village entrance is about
15–40 minutes
on foot. Where the vehicle can go depends on road construction conditions, so check with your driver. If you have a lot of luggage, you can hire a local porter.
From Sagada it's about
1 hour
to Bontoc by jeepney, then about
2–3 hours
from Bontoc to Banaue by van or jeepney, from where you enter Batad using the methods above.
The Ohayami Trans night bus from the Governor Pack Road terminal in Baguio takes about
8 hours
to reach Banaue. The return bus from Banaue to Baguio leaves at
5 PM
After a flight of about
1 hour
from Manila to Cauayan Airport (CYZ) in Isabela on Cebu Pacific or PAL Express, a chartered vehicle covers about
130km
to Banaue in roughly
3–4 hours
. It saves time if you want to avoid the night bus, but you have to pay for the vehicle charter.
After planting is finished in
January–February
, Batad's terraces turn green in
March–May
and ripen to gold for harvest in
June–July
. The most photogenic time is the deep green of
April–May
and just before harvest around
June
. In
August–December
, the paddies fill with water, mirroring the sky, or the curves of the walls stand out clearly, each with its own charm.
The dry season,
December–April
, is good for trekking, with dry trails and clear skies. Dawn temperatures in
December–February
are chilly, around
. During the rainy season,
June–October

, afternoon showers and fog are frequent, and if a typhoon comes, landslides can cut the Banaue–Batad road or make the way to the falls dangerous. Build in extra time if visiting during the rainy season.

January–March
is the driest, while in
May–September
monthly rainfall is around 400mm and it rains almost every day. In
, the fourth Tinawon rice harvest festival, "Iwang ad Batad," was held on

, with rice-wine brewing, the communal-labor tradition "bachang," traditional games, and trekking events. Tinawon means "once a year" and refers to Batad's native rice, harvested only once a year. The village sets the festival dates each year, so check the latest announcements. During Holy Week and the holiday period at the end of
December
, domestic travelers flood in and buses and guesthouses fill up early.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Several guesthouses (inns) overlooking the rice terraces are scattered around Batad village. Most are simple lodgings with shared bathrooms and basic bedding, priced at about

per night per person or per room. Guesthouses with a full view of the amphitheater sit higher up near the Saddle Point, while the quieter ones are lower in the village. There are also experiential lodgings where you can sleep in a traditional Ifugao house, so inquire in advance if you're interested. There are no convenience stores, so prepare anything you need in Banaue.

Meals are handled at the restaurant attached to your guesthouse. Basic Filipino home-style options like fried rice, eggs, sauteed vegetables, and adobo sit alongside traveler-friendly dishes like pancakes and banana shakes. Rice and vegetables grown right in the village are often used, so the food is simple but clean-tasting. It's understandable that prices run a little higher than in Banaue, since ingredients have to be carried up by hand.

Among the long-running lodgings, Ramon's Native Homestay is well known. You sleep in an old traditional Ifugao house and, together with the host family, can try on traditional clothing or pound rice with a mortar. The rooms in the traditional house have no electricity, so candles or lanterns are used. Before a trek, fried sweet potato made from sweet potatoes grown in the fields around the village makes a good snack, and guesthouses and shops sell Ifugao coffee, rice wine, and wood carvings as souvenirs. Bottled drinks and beer cost more than in Banaue because they are carried in on people's backs.
There are no ATMs in Batad. Bring cash for accommodation, meals, guide, and environmental fees, and pack a little extra.
Leave large suitcases at your Banaue accommodation and bring only an overnight backpack. Suitcases are essentially unusable on the many stone steps.
A guide isn't mandatory on every stretch, but the paddy paths are laid out like a maze, so it's recommended to go to Tappiya Falls with a guide. Guide fees also directly support the village's income.
Trekking shoes or sandals with good grip are essential. If you want to swim at the falls, bring a swimsuit and towel.
Phone signal is only available, and unreliable, in some parts of the upper village. Even guesthouses with Wi-Fi tend to be slow, so don't expect much.
Electricity is available, but there can be outages, so bring a headlamp and a portable battery.
For photos,
7–9 AM
and after
4 PM
give softer light and make the terrace tiers look more three-dimensional.

Even in Banaue town there are only a few ATMs, such as the Landbank in the municipal hall building, so if one is out of order there is no alternative. Withdraw the cash you need for your Batad trip in advance in Manila or Baguio.

You can find a guide at the Banaue tourist information center or the registration point at the Batad entrance. There is often no fixed fee schedule, so settle the route (only Tappiya Falls, or also the high viewpoint, the main village, and Awa Viewpoint) and the per-group fee before setting off.

If you chartered a tricycle, agree on the pickup time and place (the end of the road or the Saddle Point) and get the driver's phone number. Signal is weak inside the village, so it is hard to reach the driver right away.
Many of the paddy walls are narrow with large drops. Accidents really do happen from walking while looking at a phone or stepping backward to take photos, so always watch your footing.
Don't step on and collapse the paddy walls or walk into the paddies. Rebuilding even one stone wall takes a great deal of residents' labor.
The current at Tappiya Falls grows strong after rain. Don't swim directly under the falls, and follow your guide's judgment.
The climb back up from the falls is harder than it looks. Bring plenty of water, and get back to the village before dark.
Don't photograph inside residents' homes or ritual sites without permission.
Roads can be blocked by landslides during the rainy season, so it's safer to head back to Banaue the day before your return journey.
The ground is weak around the slopes hit by the
November 2025
landslides and around the irrigation channels and paddy walls under repair. Do not enter collapsed sections, and stay on the routes your guide chooses.
